articles.text: On Sunday morning, July 2, the city introduced 200 goats to the hillside behind the Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. Tasked with reducing fire hazard by eating dry vegetation on city property, the goats arrived in town after completing a shrub-eating job at the former Oak Knoll Naval Base near the Oakland Zoo. After the four-legged grazers complete their work on the slope behind the Corporation Yard, they will be moved across Moraga Avenue to Blair Park. Owned by Ecosystem Concepts, their vegetation-eating is crucial in advance of fire season. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan has said that a good rule of thumb to prevent ladder fuel — a firefighting term for vegetation which carries a fire from the landscape upward to tree or shrub canopies — is to leave three times the amount of space above the potential culprit. Thus, for one foot of grass, the goats are expected to eat enough to leave at least three feet of space between it and any tree or shrub canopies above. articles.text: In preparation for African American History Month this year, I am reading Against The Hounds of Hell: A Life of Howard Thurman by Peter Eisenstadt. I highly recommend the book. It is a definitive biography of one of the great spiritual leaders of our time. (Thurman’s most wellknown book, Jesus and the Disinherited, was, along with the Bible and United States Constitution, one of the three books that Martin Luther King Jr. carried with him when he traveled.) As the story of Thurman’s life unfolds, Eisenstadt describes the then 44-year-old pastor and scholar arriving in San Francisco in July 1944 after a five-day cross country train ride from Washington D.C. where he had been Dean of the Chapel at Howard University. After settling into a home that needed much care (think rodent infestation), Thurman began his work as the Senior Minister of the recently founded Church for the Fellowship of All People. Thurman told the church leaders that he wanted the church’s highest commitment to be to a peace rooted “in the quality of life that emanates from the place rather than from pronouncements of one kind or another.” His words describe my hope for this year’s celebration of AAHM. While it is important, especially in the face of efforts like those being made by Governor Ron DeSantis of Florida to deny the significance of African American history, that we make pronouncements about the significance of this celebration, the lessons we carry with us from the study of African American history are of greater significance than the statements we make about it. That being said, Jemar Tisby, President of the Black Christian Collective, provides five helpful pronouncements about the celebration of Black History Month. • Celebrating honors the historic leaders of the Black Community • Celebrating helps us to be better stewards of the privileges we’ve gained • Celebrating provides an opportunity to highlight the best black history and culture

articles.text: Mended Hearts, a nonprofit offering support to heart disease patients, their families, and their caregivers, is holding its annual summer barbecue picnic on Saturday, July 15, at Middle Harbor Shoreline Park in Oakland. Attendance is free and does not require membership in Mended Hearts. Those interested in attending may call Carter Dunlap at 415-298-1956 for more information and event details. The mission of Mended Hearts is to inspire hope and improve the quality of life of heart patients and their families through peerto-peer support, advocacy, and education of patients on all aspects of cardiac healthcare. Through the organization, caregivers of heart patients can get informed about their loved one’s condition and treatment options that are available. Knowing what to ask and how to ask it are important tools for everyone. If you are a heart patient or a caregiver and interested in learning more about Mended Hearts, the picnic is a great way to meet members of the chapter. The local Oakland chapter of Mended Hearts also hosts monthly meetings that feature medical professionals who inform members on relevant, up to date information about heart health care and lifestyle management. Additional information about these meetings is available on its website: mendedhearts.org.

articles.text: The Scout National Jamboree will take place this summer from July 19 to 28 at the Summit Bechtel Reserve, an area of 10,600 acres in West Virginia. Piedmont Scouts will be part of a group from Marin and will include Troop Leader Joe Anastasi (Troop 4), Travers Kemp, Samantha Pell, and Dylan Wallway of Troop 1; Nico Jerez and Joey Anastasi of Troop 4 and Diego Branneria, Ganden Deming, and Simon March-Cunningham of Troop 15. Jim Pell and his wife Siow Fang Tan will be part of the National Jamboree Service Team (staff). Piedmont Scouts will be joined by four adult leaders, and 12 Scouts from Marin. The last Jamboree took place in 2017 and was scheduled to be followed by one in 2021 but delayed due to COVID. Jamboree is a 10-day, exciting and eye-opening experience where Scouts from all over the nation can connect with each other. Starting in 1937, the first Jamboree was meant to commemorate Scouting’s 25th anniversary two years earlier. However, it was delayed two years due to a polio outbreak. Hmm… doesn’t that sound familiar? While details on the exact events of the first National Jamboree remain fuzzy, this year’s events have me squealing in excitement. While eagerly looking through the Jamboree website a few activities really stood out to me. From what I have seen, it looks like my favorite will be “The Ropes.” Thirty feet off the ground and a complex maze of floating objects and railthin bridges, it looked absolutely exhilarating. Another air suspended activity that caught my eye is “The Canopy”. It’s like the Ropes but consists almost entirely of a variety of zip lines. To be completely honest, I am absolutely in love with the idea of a zip line. To me it feels like the pinnacle of adventure. Confession: I’m also partially terrified of them. As I watched a video on mountain biking, I felt mortally terror-stricken. Here was yet another thing whose idea I love but am afraid of doing in real life. Am I really scared of the activity or is it the thought that I might mess up, or not be able to master the course within the first five seconds? But what is Jamboree? What is Scouting really all about? It’s about taking new risks, exploring, and growing as a person. I took a deep breath, pushed aside my doubts and added both “zip lining” and “mountain biking” to my ever-growing mental list of things I intend to do this July. Due to the delay of Jambo, as it’s affectionately called, many Scouts are eager to enjoy this once-in-a-lifetime experience. However, with the enormous amount of preparation, the Piedmont contingent and many others across America are practically bursting with anticipation and responsibility. According to the official National Jamboree website contingent members are expected to work together and be able to understand each other over the course of an outing or camping trip The Piedmont contingent has been meeting since last year and, even after suffering a minor setback due to a lack of female chaperones, we bounced back by collaborating with the Marin Scout Council. What exactly have we been doing to prepare for this epic adventure? We have been having meetings since last school year, and more recently, Zoom meetings with the Marin Scouts. Additionally, we have been arranging a potential day outing and camping trip. I have been putting together packing lists and charts on the activities I want to do. I have set aside clothes and raised money. A huge thank you to everyone who donated and bought my cookies. I could not have dreamed of doing this without them. I’m getting ready for one of the best summers of my life, so keep your eyes on The Post to follow our adventure. Samantha Pell is a member of Piedmont Scout Troop 1, and an intern with the Piedmont Post. HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

articles.text: Have you ever felt frustrated during meal times? Have you spent 20 minutes attempting to convince a three-year-old master negotiator to eat “just a tiny little bite” of cauliflower? Have you drowned green beans in cheese? Have you hid miniscule shreds of butternut squash in macaroni in cheese, praying that your child won’t notice your trickery? If so, you are not alone. From birth, babies are expected to do two things: eat and breathe. The majority of time that most parents spend with their newborns and young children revolve around food. With the time it takes to prepare food, feed kids, and clean up, it is a miracle that parents of young children have time for anything else. The CDC recommends feeding toddlers and young children at least six (YES…SIX) times per day. This means that when feeding becomes a challenge, parents can feel like they are “failing” six times per day. While a majority of toddlers and young children experience a certain degree of “picky eating” as a part of their typical development, there is a line where strict food restrictions and aversions can become dangerous and indicative of an underlying condition, such as Pediatric Feeding Disorder. Here are six signs that your child’s limited diet may be more than just “picky eating” and may be signs of “problem feeding”: 1. Sudden or significant weight loss or failure to gain or maintain weight: If your child is losing weight, or having trouble gaining the expected amount of weight for their age, it is recommended that you consult with your pediatrician to ensure that there is not a serious underlying cause. 2. Limited diet of less than 30 foods: Problem feeders present with a significantly restricted range and variety of tolerated foods, typically less than 30 foods. 3. Eating the same food over and over, then suddenly stopping eating that food: A “food jag” is a typical developmental pattern that occurs when a child eats the same foods prepared in the same way, every day or at every meal. Eventually they are likely to get burned out on these foods and they are usually lost from the child’s diet permanently. Picky Eaters will normally accept and eat that food after taking a two week break without eating it but Problem Feeders will rarely ever accept that food again, even after taking a break. 4. Crying, yelling, running away from the table when new/nonpreferred foods are presented: Picky eaters will typically tolerate novel or nonpreferred foods in their vicinity. On the other hand, problem feeders may cry, protest, or “fall apart” when presented with new or nonpreferred foods. 5. Refusing entire food groups or only eating foods of similar textures/shapes/colors: Picky Eaters will eat at least one food from most food texture/ nutrition groups (i.e., starch, protein/dairy, fruit/vegetable). However, Problem Feeders will refuse to eat entire categories of food textures or nutrition groups. 6. Consistent picky eating: Problem Feeders are persistently reported by a parent as a “picky eater” across multiple well-child check-ups, typically for more than two years. If your child presents with one or more of these signs, your child may be a Problem Feeder. Please consult with your pediatrician for a referral to a feeding specialist. articles.text: Piedmont resident Josh Bernstein, a lifelong swimmer, has turned a hobby into an activity that motivates him every day, typically starting at daybreak. He is perhaps Piedmont’s most celebrated open water swimmer, routinely swimming under the Golden Gate Bridge and from Alcatraz to the city. At age 66 he is just getting started. To prove the point, he recently was part of a six-person relay team from South End Rowing Club in San Francisco that swam the storied English Channel, an open water swim of approximately 21 miles from Dover, England to Calais, France. To prepare, he swam the aquatic version of the Bay to Breakers race – from the Bay Bridge to the Golden Gate Bridge. – Josh Bernstein Bernstein’s group crossed the channel in 13 hours, 58 minutes amidst less than ideal conditions. After 12 days of delays due to weather and high waves, his group was given the go-ahead to enter the water on June 29. “We had a window from June 17 to July 2 and we were hoping to swim earlier in the window just to put it behind us, described Bernstein. “We didn’t get to swim due to the conditions until June 29 and there were a couple of false alarms, too. We were called four days prior and were set to start at 2:00 a.m., but we got a call at midnight saying conditions wouldn’t allow.’ ‘I learned very quickly when we were out there that conditions Josh Bernstein recently completed the challenging swim across the English Channel between England and France. can get gnarly,” he added. Bernstein, Bill Wygant, Susan Blew, Conny Bleul, Carol Merryfield, and Jen Karlin began their swim at 6:10 p.m., four hours before darkness set in, rotating swimmers on one-hour intervals. A boat from the Channel Swimming Association carried each of them and whistled when it was time for them to switch. “It was rough right off of the bat for the first swimmer, but then it mellowed out for a few hours. As the evening wore on, conditions really got rough with big whitecap swells and it was dark, cold, and windy. Plus we’re sleepy because we were staying up all night. But we had a great team with a lot of experience,” said Bernstein. “Shortly after we arrived in Dover, a swimmer who was going solo died. He just disappeared under the waves and they couldn’t find him, he was near France at the time. It was really tragic, and a harsh reminder that what we were about to undertake was no small thing. It wasn’t going for a little swim. We all knew it was a big deal,” said Bernstein. “I had to really keep in mind to keep an eye on the boat and try not to worry about the jellyfish. There were tons and tons of jellyfish and they sting. I’m fortunate to not react heavily to jellyfish other than it stings for a moment, I didn’t get a lasting rash but several people on our team did. There’s also a condition called Salt Tongue and it can cause your tongue to swell up so much that you can’t eat or drink. Several of our swimmers got mild cases of it, I luckily didn’t get either,” said Bernstein. Bernstein’s team followed a current along the channel, following its bending path arcing from north to south. “We’re all seasoned open-water swimmers and we know what our long distance pace is, so we just kept that for an hour. We followed the current and our path was one of the flattest curves I’ve seen for a channel crossing. It’s usually a huge dip north, a huge dip south, then another dip to the north. [The organizers] picked a good time for us to swim because the current was a little bit mellow,” said Bernstein. articles.text: Following the Coastal Trail with a pit stop at Pelican Inn Tennessee Valley Beach and Muir Beach are among the most popular destinations in Marin County, so why not connect them for your own beach-hopping excursion? Walking the Coastal Fire Road trail gives some tough leg-work with ascending and descending elevation, but provides a beautiful jaunt along the Pacific Ocean. The Post’s Hiking with Jon series starts at the Tennessee Valley Beach trailhead, taking the main path until intersecting with the Coastal Trail after a mile, walking roughly 3.1 miles to Muir Beach with around 1,000 feet in elevation gain. According to historians, Muir Beach itself was once known as Bello Beach when Portuguese settler Antonio Nunez Bello bought the entire hillside for a $10 gold piece in 1910. About 2.4 miles from the Tennessee Valley Trailhead, you’ll pass Pirates Cove, a small boulder laden beach surrounded by steep hills. It requires about 350 feet of descent from the main trail and will provide a leg-burner of a walk back up. The remaining 1.8 miles to Muir Beach, hikers will pass bushels of stunning red-flowering currant and possibly spot a rabbit or two hopping across the trail. Large turkey vultures are a common sight throughout the Marin Headlands, while you may see a red-tailed hawk scouring for food. After the grueling walk, take a rest at Muir Beach or cool off with your feet in the cold ocean Follow the signs to Muir Beach. Tennessee Valley Beach is on the left as seen from the Coastal Fire Road trail. The walk along the coast is picturesque, and depending on the weather, you can see the marine layer of clouds burning off over the hills. Take time for lunch and a pint at the historic Pelican Inn for prior to heading back.

articles.text: San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) celebrates Black beauty and femininity with Black Venus, on view now through August 20. The exhibition is curated by Aindrea Emelife and is a reflection of the legacy of Black Women in visual culture, from colonial-era caricatures to the reclamation of Black womanhood by 18 artists of numerous nationalities and ages. Artwork spans from 1793 to the present day. Featured artists include Alberta Whittle, Amber Pinkerton, Ayana V. Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, Carla Williams, Coreen Simpson, Deana Lawson, Deborah Roberts, Frida Orupabo, Ming Smith, Kara Walker, Maud Sulter, Lorna Simpson, Renee Cox, Sadie Barnette, Shawanda Corbett, Tabita Rezaire, Taiye Idahor, Wangechi Mutu, Yetunde Olagbaju and Zanele Muholi. The museum advises visitors that some artwork contains sensitive and difficult imagery, as well as depictions of nudity. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus, a visual-culture archetype named for the assigned stage name of Saartje Baartman (born 1789 in South Africa), fetishised by Dutch colonizers and slave traders. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/black-venus. articles.text: Diego Rivera’s famous fresco piece, “Pan American Unity,” will remain on view to the public at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art until March 2024. On June 17, 2021, Diego Rivera’s colossal fresco “Pan American Unity” was carefully moved from San Francisco City College to SFMOMA. The priceless 4,000-pound series of panels, created in 1940, is arguably one of San Francisco’s greatest art pieces of the 20th century. Rivera’s mural was the centerpiece of the Art in Action exhibit, which featured different artists engaged in creating art pieces while the public watched. The fresco on plaster measures 670 by 2,260 centimeters and was created on 10 robust steel-framed panels bolted together and weighing about 21 tons. It was designed to be portable, and was moved to the college campus from Treasure Island after the end of the World’s Fair. It is the largest of the artist’s works, and completely spanned the narrow lobby of the college’s Diego Rivera Theater. A four-year, multimillion dollar undertaking resulted in its careful removal and transport across the city to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, where it officially went on display. In partnership with City College, SFMOMA presents Rivera’s “Pan American Unity” in the museum free to the public until March 2024, when it will then return to City College to be installed in a new performing arts center. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pan-american-unity/ to learn more. Diego Rivera’s famous fresco piece “Pan American Unity”

articles.text: Performances of Hurricane Diane at Berkeley’s Aurora Theatre will continue through July 16. The play by Madeleine George follows protagonist Carol, a seemingly ordinary if not materialistic woman who resides on a New Jersey cul-de-sac. One day, she is visited by the Greek god Dionysus, under the guise of a lesbian gardener named Diane. Diane is determined to reverse climate change and restore earthly order by seducing a band of mortal followers, and sets out to woo Carol from her picture-perfect suburban life. articles.text: To become an accomplished physician requires dedication, long hours, and a strong love for the art of medicine. This is also true of becoming an accomplished musician. To be both is remarkable. Meet Joel Richmon, MD. Born into an extended family of many physicians, he followed suit and graduated from medical school at the University of Rochester in 1965. He completed his internship and residency at Johns Hopkins and his training in neurology at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Beth Israel Hospital in Boston. Having finished his training in 1971, Richmon moved to Piedmont and joined the Internal Medicine Department at Kaiser Oakland. A few years later, he was appointed as the hospital’s first chief of the Department of Neurology at Kaiser Oakland. In 1995 he established the first Headache Clinic at Kaiser. He retired from Kaiser in 2001, after 30 years of medical practice. Richmon’s musical career has its roots in his extended family. As a young boy, he lived in Waukegan, Illinois with his maternal grandmother and his aunt Janet Eisenberg, who loved to play classical piano. He recounts the story that his crib was often placed under his aunt’s piano, which she played every day. Her playing never failed to soothe him and germinated his love for classical piano. At the age of nine, Richmon started formal lessons in Chicago and studied with the distinguished Russian teacher Vitaly Schnee. At age 19, he continued his studies with Dr. Rudolph Ganz, president of the Chicago Musical College. He continued playing and practicing through medical school and residency, even arranging for his piano to be moved to Johns Hopkins. Before leaving to begin his career in Oakland, Joel played two pieces for Dr. Ganz, who told him, “My boy, you have two careers.” Richmon continued his studies in California with famed piano scholar Adolph Baller in Palo Alto. He has previously performed with members of the Oakland Symphony Orchestra and the San Francisco Symphony, as well as the faculty of the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. In 1977 Richmon had his most memorable experience as a musician, He admired Gitta Gradova, a world-famous concert pianist who abruptly retired from performing in 1941. She dropped out of the public eye and married Dr. Maurice Cottle, a renowned otolaryngologist and an accomplished amateur violinist. Coincidentally, a friend of Richmon’s was also a friend of the Cottles, and he arranged for Richmon to visit them in Chicago so he could “fulfill his dream of playing the piano” for her. Richmon wrote at the time: “In the Cottles’ drawing room sat two Steinway concert grand pianos positioned back-to-back across the room from each other. My hostess briefly remarked that one of the pianos was the favorite of Horowitz; the other, the favorite of Ashkenazy. Humbly and in awe, I seated myself at one of the storied pianos and played Rachmaninoff’s Second Piano Sonata, after which Mrs. Cottle graciously offered me her expert critique. Then, with an unbelievably sumptuous tonal quality, she played for me an excerpt from the beautiful, slow movement of Schumann’s Piano Quartet in E-flat Major. Mrs. Cottle gave Richmon one more gift, and that was the suggestion to play chamber music. This led him to a collaboration with other accomplished musicians and opened a new area of classical music for him. A year later, Joel held his first recital at the Berkeley Piano Club, where he played two pieces of chamber music with other musicians and two solo works. This was the first of 10 recitals, most of them held at Holy Names University in Oakland, performed for family and friends, including Kaiser colleagues. His latest and final recital was held on March 26, 2023, at Hertz Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. An estimated 400 to 500 people heard him perform Bach’s Piano Concerto No. 5 in F minor and his Piano Concerto No. 1 in D minor with the members of the Oakland Symphony conducted by Bryan Nies. He also performed Franck’s Prelude, Fugue and Variation in B minor, Op. 18, Liszt’s Funerailles, and Chopin’s Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op.52. Each piece was saluted by the applause of an enthusiastic audience. Richmon entertained audiences with stories about his Aunt Janet, to whom he dedicated the recital in March. He listed Elvis, Janis Joplin, Van Cliburn with the Chicago Grant Park Symphony, and trumpeter Chet Baker in Paris as his favorite concerts. Richmon will continue to play and entertain friends. After all, it’s what he loves. Piedmont resident Joel Richmon, a retired physician, plays his last recital with the Oakland Symphony at Hertz Hall on the UC Berkeley campus on March 26.
articles.title: Retired MD plays final recital with Oakland Symphony

articles.text: Robert Capron, Zachary Gordon, and Chloë Grace Moretz in Diary of a Wimpy Kid You’re 12-years-old, on the cusp of that long, tortuous road known as adolescence, and it’s the first day of middle school. Middle school is like Triple A ball before you get called up to the big show, also known as high school. Meanwhile, there’s a lot to learn because, well, look around, everyone’s changing. No one’s a kid any longer. But then, no one’s a serious teenager either. Middle school is purgatory. Weird and awkward, it can be brutal. Which is the point of Diary of a Wimpy Kid, based on the popular illustrated books by Jeff Kinney. The movie should have been rich with material about kids trying to figure out not only who they are but how things work. This is not elementary school. There are no white lines on the tarmac, no recess, no tetherball or games of four-square or tag. Adios to those comfy classrooms with Nancy the hamster in that cage filled with sawdust and shredded newspapers and the walls covered with colored paper, the alphabet strung in an arc above the large-face clock and a few friendly admonitions on the bulletin board next to exemplary homework assignments. So Diary of a Wimpy Kid easily could have been comedic, insightful and, well, fun. It isn’t. For reasons that are difficult to understand. Perhaps it’s not possible to take Kinney’s book to the screen. But how to understand that the central character, Greg Heffley (Zach Gordon), is neither wimpy nor sympathetic; rather, he’s a self-absorbed, dishonest kid whose mission is to become instantly popular and is willing to do whatever it takes. His older brother, an older version of Greg, tries to explain the middle school rules: Don’t get noticed. Don’t go to the bathroom. Try and be cool. And speaking of cool, Greg is constantly on the verge of ditching his best friend, Rowley (Robert Capron), who is so endearingly dorky that he’s impossible not to like. But since Greg is in the hunt for cool, he cringes at how un-cool Rowley is. As example when the two are leaving school, Rowley yells from the top of the steps, with older kids everywhere, “Hey Greg, wanna come over and play?” Greg wants to hide because he knows that in middle school no one plays. Cool kids hang out. Later, when Greg is confronted with a moment of truth, he sells Rowley out and never looks back. He’s not a good friend. a conclusion, Greg is a well-established creep. And even with a final 10 minutes for an epiphany, with redemption for Greg at the edge of the school grounds, it all seems a bit contrived and too late. He’s not a kid you want to hang out with. All of these kids have an interior life, one filled with questions and confusion and insecurities; however, nothing in depth is ever really explored. Diary of a Wimpy Kid shoulda, coulda been a serious/funny/ touching movie, helped perhaps by a nice voice over. And not to forget honest. It’s not; it’s another missed opportunity. articles.text: Studio 415 Interiors – helping Piedmonters feel right at home Since creating their interior design firm Studio 415 three years ago, Piedmonter Beatriz Martinez and Hailey Johnson have been making their clients’ dream spaces a reality. Originally from Cuernavaca, south of Mexico City, Martinez earned her bachelor’s degree in architecture from Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City in 1995, and a master’s degree in interior design from Pratt Institute in New York in 1997. Having then worked for two years at New York City design firm Skidmore Owings & Merrill, she moved to San Francisco and joined the hospitality design firm BraytonHughes in 1999, working there on and off until founding Studio 415 in 2020. “When we started during the pandemic,” said Martinez, “everyone was locked down and looking for home offices, and we found a design niche we didn’t know existed. I decided to start a company. Hailey, who I used to work with at BraytonHughes in San Francisco, joined me.” Johnson, who grew up in Pleasanton, earned a bachelor’s degree in Interior Design from San Francisco State University. “I know not many kids can say this, but from a very young age I loved floor plans,” she said. “I was always moving friends’ furniture around and knew I wanted to go for the interior design route.” Though she joined BraytonHughes and met Martinez in 2016, she moved to New York to do hospitality design work for InterContinental Hotels. “With Studio 415, Bea gave me an opportunity to return to San Francisco that I couldn’t pass up,” said Johnson. “Though I loved New York, my heart and life is in the Bay, and I came back in spring 2020. “At our studio we provide a full range of interior design services from design drawings, permit packages, design selections, to turn-key installations,” she added. The entire process for a large project, from the permit phase to the end of design, often takes two years or more. Though the pair are working on 10 projects at any given time, they’ve moved from their hospitality background to a strong focus on residential design. “My favorite part of the residential work is that much of it depends on knowing your clients really well on a personal, individual level — what colors and patterns make them feel the best, and how they live in their own spaces overall,” said Martinez. Some of their current projects include a commercial motorcycle shop in San Francisco, a private residence in Temescal, two in the Oakland Hills, and an upcoming kitchen, bathroom, and dining room remodel in Piedmont. articles.text: Nancy DeRoche offered to take the group on a tour of her neighborhood above Oakland Avenue, which includes historic Blair and Scenic Avenues. Nancy told the group she became interested in the history of her neighborhood, and has used the research of Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi. The area above Oakland Avenue was a bit of a Bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters, including Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there in some unique homes. Some of them built their own homes. Nancy led the group to the home of George Sterling, who was Frank C. Havens’ nephew. Sterling was a frustrated artist and poet and traveled in a circle of artists. He met Jack London and encouraged London to live in Piedmont. As the walkers were making their climb of Blair, Nancy pointed out the Sutro Mansion at the top of the street, hidden by other homes. The mansion was not the first house on this hilltop site. Initially, a much smaller, craftsman-style home was built there in 1876-77 by Joseph Worcester. This house has a special claim to fame. It was there that Jack London lived and wrote his classic novel, The Call of the Wild, in 1902-03. After London lived there, the house was moved two lots up the street in 1910 so that the Sutro mansion could be built and have expansive views of the Bay. The house. It has a lovely, cedar shake shingle exterior, and was enlarged after it was moved by adding a new first floor. London was a prominent part of the artists’ colony that occupied this part of Piedmont in the early 1900s. He was a free-spirited man who sailed to the Orient, drank freely, and had at least three important women in his life. The success of The Call of the Wild provided him with considerable wealth. He built a separate home for first wife, Bessie, and their two daughters on Scenic Avenue. The walkers continued up Scenic, went past Bessie’s home, and stopped at a turn in the bend of the street to enjoy the view of San Francisco and the Bay. As they were admiring the view, longtime resident Karen Eliassen welcomed the group to the view. The group made their way up to the Scenic loop and came to the rustic bungalow home of another famous member of the Piedmont Bohemian community, painter Xavier Martinez. This home/studio was inhabited by his daughter and artist, Kai Martinez, until her death in 1989. The group made their way down the narrow part of Scenic and decided to have an adventure on their way home, descending the hill via Piedmont’s longest pedestrian pathway and set of stairs, the 281-foot Blair and Scenic Path. All of the walkers safely got back to Blair, and then down to Pacific and Mountain Avenues to the Community Hall parking lot. The group gave Nancy a round of applause at the walk’s end for the wonderful tour of her historic neighborhood. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. And there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required.at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.
